title: Frequency-aware Dynamic Gaussian Splatting
claim: Standard kernels need dense stacking and smooth out fast motion; differentiating kernels by frequency lets each follow fine-grained dynamics without blur.
layout: Image crops left, two schematic panels right; t=1 over t=2 rows, red vs blue
description: The left side shows a rendered person in a yellow top at two timesteps, t=1 and t=2. A red box marks the hand, with zoomed crops. Each crop pairs a blurry Baseline (red border) with a sharper Ours (blue border), joined by dashed lines. The right side has two schematic panels on grey. Panel (a) Baseline has a red border. It shows many overlapping orange dashed Gaussian ellipses along a curved black contour, with yellow-brown downward arrows for low-frequency deformation at t=1 and t=2. Panel (b) Ours has a blue border. It shows a few large low-frequency kernels plus a small high-frequency kernel, with brown and green arrows for low- and high-frequency deformation. A legend explains the kernel types and arrow colors. A bottom caption reads 'High-frequency details and high-frequency motion'.
caption: Analysis of high-frequency details and motion. (a) Baseline: Standard Gaussian kernels require dense overlapping to capture high-frequency details, which complicates deformation control and biases the network toward smooth, low-frequency trajectories, resulting in motion blur. (b) Our method: Gaussians in highand low-frequency regions are differentiated, enabling the deformation network to capture high-frequency motion on top of global low-frequency deformations, allowing each Gaussian to follow its own fine-grained dynamics. thereby reducing reliance on dense Gaussian stacking. Second, the Fourier-Deformation Network models motion trajectories as a superposition of periodic movements at multiple frequencies. By learning the amplitude distribution of highand low-frequency components, it enables precise motion estimation—capturing rapid, high-frequency displacements over short intervals while maintaining stable, low-frequency trends globally. abstract: We present \textbf{Frequency-Aware Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (FAGS)}, a novel approach to mitigating motion blur in 4D reconstruction, particularly under novel viewpoints. This blur stems from a fundamental spectral conflict in existing methods, which struggle to \textbf{balance high-frequency rendering details with high-frequency motion.} FAGS addresses this challenge with two key innovations. First, we introduce a frequency-differentiated Gaussian kernel that refines the alpha-blending process of 3D Gaussian Splatting. By adaptively classifying Gaussians into two types—a slowly varying kernel for smooth, low-frequency regions and a sharp-transitioning kernel for high-frequency boundaries—our method explicitly separates representation responsibilities, preserving fine details without sacrificing continuity. Second, we propose a Fourier-Deformation Network that enhances motion expressiveness. This network employs high-frequency Fourier embeddings to capture diverse motion patterns by learning amplitudes across frequency components. To further improve accuracy, we integrate a frequency-aware gate in fusion module, which predicts and regulates the relative deformation of each Gaussian. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world 4D benchmarks demonstrate that FAGS significantly reduces motion blur and enhances structural details, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
